newsitem.title: USA: U.S. utilities say FERC tariff proposal premature.
newsitem.headline: U.S. utilities say FERC tariff proposal premature.

text.p: U.S. utilities on Friday poured cold water on an idea by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to require all transmission line owners to file a capacity reservation tariff by the end of 1997.

The commission had thought a capacity reservation tariff might be the best way to promote efficient use of the electric grid as power markets became more competitive under the FERC's open transmission access rules that went into effect in July.
With a reservation tariff, transmission users would have to book firm rights between specific points on the grid instead of booking space based on total load requirements.

While the commission believed that the capacity reservation system would allow all market participants to know how much and where capacity was available at any time, utility officials told FERC the system might not work that way.

"Moving to a CRT (capacity reservation tariff) is neither technically feasible nor economically desirable," said Charles Bayless, CEO of Tucson Electric Power Co, who represented the Edison Electric Institute at a FERC conference on the proposal.
FERC hoped that reservation rights would help spur a secondary market for trading transmission capacity.
But utility officials said trading physical transmission rights could complicate coordination of power production and transmission operations which are already complex.

"The proposal ... to create a reservation system and tradeable rights based on specific physical performance would be extremely difficult to implement and could have undesirable consequences, particularly the creation of stranded transmission costs," said Paul McCoy, a vice president of Commonwealth Edison Co, unit of Unicom Corp.

Industry officials also warned that any new tariff designed to allocate transmission capacity should only be put in place after utilities have set up independent system operators with authority to redispatch power and manage trading of capacity rights.

A capacity reservation tariff would likely spur power producers to overbook transmission capacity so that they are guaranteed space during peak demand periods, said John Odom, an engineer at Florida Power Corp, a unit of Florida Progress Corp.
Overestimates of the capacity needed would lead to inefficient use of transmission space, he said.

Utility officials and a state representative urged the commission to let states and regional power pools experiment with new approaches for allocating transmission capacity, instead of imposing a single, untried tariff on all utilities in the next 15 months.
